I feel like incomplete data from so many sources can cause mistrust too. Even with the first example with the skin cream, I paused the video to answer it. My instant reaction was that it was the no cream based on proportion. Then, I thought the answer might be that it's a trick question because the intensity of being better or worse wasn't given. No cream may still be the correct answer but if "rash improved" for the skin cream was intense and the "rash worsened" was intense for the no cream, I might make a different decision whether to use the cream or not in a practical situation.I would imagine that the more complex the scenario (like gun control), the more variables there are that aren't presented. Wouldn't that cause people to not trust the data given and just go with their intuition? Or even intuition of the tribe?

When I first encountered the question, I paused the video and calculated the natural course of the disease for patients with this skin condition who received no treatment at all. For simplicity, I rounded the numbers so that out of 125 untreated patients, 20 got worse and 105 improved. This gives roughly 84% improvement — meaning that, on average, a patient’s condition progresses according to this standard without any treatment.Then I looked at the table for patients who received cream treatment: out of 300 patients, 225 improved and 75 got worse. Here, the average improvement rate dropped to 75%, which suggested that the cream treatment actually made the patients worse.However, if we reverse the numbers for the untreated group — saying that out of 125 untreated patients, 105 got worse and only 20 improved — then the natural course of the disease shows only a 16% improvement rate. In the cream group, if 225 out of 300 got worse and 75 improved, the improvement rate becomes 25%. In this case, we could conclude that the cream treatment actually helped the patients.You could say this question is a good test for whether someone can stop and think carefully enough to perform the correct statistical calculation. But in my opinion, it is not very successful at measuring “irrational intelligence.”

top_negative_comments.text: 0:35 btw if it was real experiment, the control group would still apply a fake cream containing most of the "filler" ingredients but not the actual medicine.

So, this title is VERY misleading. Without spoiling it, it is NOT supported by the evidence in this video that there exist math problems on which smarter people do worse than less smart people. What it is saying is that there exist math problems with a certain trait on which smarter people do worse than THOSE SAME SMARTER PEOPLE would have done on other, analogous math problems without that certain trait.
